```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 100)
```

Latent profile analysis (LPA) is a person-centred statistical approach used to identify unobserved subpopulations within a heterogeneous population. It assumes that the observed data arise from a finite mixture of latent profiles, each characterized by a distinct pattern of means across a set of continuous indicators. Rather than assuming that all observations originate from a single homogeneous population, LPA allows individuals to differ in their underlying response patterns and estimates the number and characteristics of the latent profiles, their relative proportions, and the posterior probability of each observation belonging to each profile. From a statistical perspective, LPA is a finite Gaussian mixture model in which the observed distribution is represented as a weighted combination of profile-specific multivariate normal distributions (Scrucca et al., 2024).

Conventional LPA assumes that observations are independent of one another. This assumption may be inappropriate when the data have a hierarchical structure, in which observations are nested within higher-level units. For example, courses completed by the same students or employees belonging to the same departments may exhibit similarities arising from their shared context. Such dependencies may also result in differences in the distribution of latent profiles across groups. Multilevel latent profile analysis extends the conventional model by accounting for heterogeneity at both the individual and group levels (Vermunt, 2003; Asparouhov & Muthén, 2008; Mäkikangas et al., 2018).

In multilevel LPA, individuals are classified into latent profiles based on their patterns across the observed indicators, while groups are classified into latent group classes according to the distribution of individual-level profiles within them. Consequently, the model captures not only differences between individuals but also systematic differences in the composition of groups. For example, two groups may contain individuals belonging to the same set of latent profiles but differ in the relative proportions of individuals assigned to each profile. These differences are represented through group-specific profile probabilities.

Formally, let $C_{ij}$ denote the latent profile membership of observation $i$ in group $j$, and let $G_j$ denote the latent group class of group $j$. The composition of each group class is described by the conditional profile probabilities:

$$
\pi_{k\mid m}=P(C_{ij}=k\mid G_j=m),
\qquad
\sum_k\pi_{k\mid m}=1.
$$

Here, $\pi_{k\mid m}$ represents the probability that an observation belongs to individual-level profile $k$, conditional on its group belonging to group class $m$. These probabilities therefore characterize the distribution of individual-level profiles within each group class. Groups assigned to different group classes may consequently differ in their profile composition, even when the underlying individual-level profiles are identical.

An important feature of this specification is that the profile-specific means and variances are assumed to remain invariant across group classes. In other words, the individual-level profiles retain the same measurement characteristics regardless of the group class in which they occur. Differences between group classes are therefore expressed through the relative prevalence of individual-level profiles rather than through changes in the profiles' underlying definitions. This constraint provides a common measurement structure for comparing group classes and facilitates the interpretation of differences in their profile compositions.

Houle et al. (2026) provide an overview of multilevel latent profile analysis and its extensions, including alternative specifications that allow additional sources of heterogeneity at the individual and group levels. In the `latents` package, the function `multilpa()` estimates the multilevel latent profile model using maximum likelihood estimation and the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm (Dempster et al., 1977). The algorithm alternates between estimating posterior probabilities of latent class membership and updating the model parameters until convergence is reached.

The analysis below proceeds in the usual order: the extent of nesting, a
first model, a check of its assumptions, the numbers of profiles and group
classes, interpretation and evaluation of the chosen model, and the relation
of its classes to another variable.

## Data

`course_engagement` contains 1,422 course enrolments of 106 students.

- **Group:** `student`.
- **Indicators:** five activity measures (`browse`, `lectures`, `forum_read`,
  `forum_post`, `attendance`), standardized within course (0 is the course
  mean, 1 one standard deviation above it).
- **External variable:** `previous_grade`, the standardized grade of the
  preceding course.

Two further columns hold the generating structure, `engagement` for each
enrolment and `student_type` for each student; they serve only to check
recovery.

```{r setup}
library(latents)
vars <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
```

## Clustering within groups

`descriptives()` summarizes the indicators and their intraclass correlation
(`icc`), the share of variance between groups, estimated from the one-way
analysis of variance (Shrout & Fleiss, 1979).

```{r descriptives}
descriptives(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student")
```

Between 9% (`lectures`) and 22% (`forum_read`, `attendance`) of the variance
lies between students. Enrolments of one student are therefore not
independent, and the students are the independent units of the analysis.
Most of the variance remains within students, where the profiles operate.

## A first model

`n_profiles` and `n_group_classes` set the numbers of profiles and group
classes; `n_starts` sets the number of EM starts, `seed` makes them
reproducible and `cores` runs them in parallel. The default covariance
structure is `"VVI"` (Celeux & Govaert, 1995): profile-specific variances and
no covariances within profiles, so the indicators are independent given the
profile.

```{r fit}
fit <- multilpa(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student",
                n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2, n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
fit
```

Profile 1 (58.7% of the enrolments) lies 0.43 to 0.65 standard deviations
above the course mean on all indicators and profile 2 (41.3%) 0.61 to 0.92
below it: engaged and disengaged enrolments. The BIC uses the 106 students as
its sample size. All ten starts reached the same log likelihood.

## Checking local independence

Under a diagonal structure, any association between indicators within a
profile can only be represented by additional profiles, which then describe
the association rather than types of observations. The `"residuals"` table
compares each within-profile association with the value the model implies,
with p-values adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini &
Hochberg, 1995).

```{r residuals}
head(get_results(fit, "residuals"), 6)
```

The six largest residuals all involve `attendance`, in both profiles: its
within-profile correlations with the other measures are 0.17 to 0.23, with
adjusted p-values below 0.00001. The data documentation confirms the source:
attendance is generated from the four click measures (`?course_engagement`).
`covariance_model = "full"` estimates all within-profile covariances
(`"VVV"`); `local_dependence` frees selected pairs.

```{r full}
full <- multilpa(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student",
                 n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
                 covariance_model = "full", n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
compare_models(diagonal = fit, full = full)
```

The full structure adds 20 parameters and lowers the BIC by 160 (BIC weight
1.000). The profiles and group classes retain their sizes and meaning; the
numbers of classes are chosen under this structure.

## Choosing the numbers of profiles and group classes

`enumerate_classes()` fits every combination of the requested numbers of
profiles and group classes and returns information criteria, classification
statistics and estimation checks. For the group classes, Lukočienė et al.
(2010) recommend the BIC (Schwarz, 1978) with the number of groups as sample
size (`bic_groups`). Group classes require at least two profiles, so
candidates with one profile and several group classes fail by design.

```{r enumerate}
grid <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student",
                          covariance_model = "full", n_profiles = 1:3,
                          n_group_classes = 1:4, n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
grid
```

`get_deltas()` gives the improvement of each criterion when a profile or a
group class is added.

```{r deltas}
subset(get_deltas(grid), criterion == "bic_groups")
```

Two profiles are supported unambiguously: the second profile lowers the BIC by
343, and a third raises it at every number of group classes, by 55 to 67.
For the group classes, the second lowers the BIC by 344, the third by 26 and
the fourth by 3, while group-level separation declines (relative entropy
0.942, 0.816 and 0.797; lowest group average posterior 0.971, 0.903 and
0.830). The AWE (Banfield & Raftery, 1993) and the ICL computed on the
enrolments (Biernacki et al., 2000), which penalize uncertain classification,
select two group classes (`get_best(grid)`). The model with two profiles and
two group classes is retained. The small gains of further group classes have
an identifiable source: engagement changes along each student's course
sequence, a dependence that multilevel LPA does not model and that additional
group classes partly absorb; `lta()` models the sequence directly (see the
[latent transition analysis](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/lta.html)
article).

Two candidates with three profiles (two and four group classes) raise
warnings: one profile has too little membership for its 20 free means and
covariances, and both reached their best likelihood from a single start.
The AIC, whose penalty is the weakest, favours three profiles with four group
classes; the BIC rejects three profiles at every number of group classes, so
the warnings do not affect the choice by BIC.

## The chosen model

```{r chosen}
full
```

Profile 1 (59.0%) lies 0.42 to 0.63 standard deviations above the course
mean and profile 2 (41.0%) 0.61 to 0.91 below it; attendance and forum reading
separate the profiles most, lecture viewing least. `get_results()` returns
the means and variances, `get_results(full, "covariances")` the covariances.

```{r profiles}
get_results(full)
```

All variances are below 1, the variance of the standardized indicators:
enrolments within a profile are more homogeneous than the sample. The profile
plot shows the means, with the profile shares in the labels.

```{r profile-plot}
plot_profiles(full)
```

### Group classes

The `"profile_probabilities"` table gives $\pi_{k \mid m}$ (`probability`) and
the proportion of groups in each class (`group_class_probability`).

```{r profile-probabilities}
get_results(full, "profile_probabilities")
```

Group class 2 (67.5% of the students) has 79.3% engaged enrolments and group
class 1 (32.5%) 16.4%: mostly engaged and mostly disengaged students. Neither
class is pure: a mostly engaged student is disengaged in about one course in
five, a mostly disengaged student engaged in about one in six. Students are mixtures of profiles in class-specific proportions. The prevalence plot shows these
probabilities.

```{r probability-plot}
plot_prevalence(full)
```

## Class sizes and classification

`effective_count` sums the posterior probabilities and is therefore not
necessarily an integer.

```{r counts}
get_results(full, "counts")
```

The profiles hold 838.8 and 583.2 enrolments, the group classes 34.5 and 71.5
students; no class is small enough to threaten estimation. Relative entropy
measures the separation of the classes on a scale from 0 (no separation) to 1
(certain assignment) (Ramaswamy et al., 1993); it is not a measure of fit.

```{r entropy}
get_results(full, "entropy")
```

Relative entropy is 0.906 for the enrolments and 0.942 for the students. The
average posterior probability of the assigned class gives the same
information by class.

```{r average-posteriors}
get_results(full, "average_posteriors")
```

The average posteriors are 0.978 and 0.973 for the profiles and 0.971 and
0.993 for the group classes. Assignments are therefore accurate at both
levels, although analyses of assigned classes still ignore the remaining
uncertainty; the three-step methods below account for it. The
`"assignments"` table adds the most probable `profile` and `group_class`, the
`uncertainty` of the profile assignment and the posterior probabilities to the
data.

```{r assignments}
get_results(full, "assignments", data = course_engagement) |> head()
```

The first student's first two enrolments are assigned to the engaged
profile, the second with an uncertainty of 0.148, and the next four to the
disengaged profile with uncertainties below 0.001; the student belongs to the
mostly disengaged group class.

## Recovery of the known structure

The `truth` argument cross-tabulates the assignments with the generating
labels; class numbers are arbitrary, so correspondence is read from the table.

```{r recovery}
get_results(full, "assignments", data = course_engagement,
            truth = c("engagement", "student_type"))
```

Profile 1 contains 824 of the 837 engaged enrolments and profile 2 567 of the
585 disengaged ones (98% and 97%). Group class 2 contains 61 of the 62
committed students but also 10 of the 44 wavering ones. The model classifies the students with high certainty (relative entropy
0.942), yet recovers the wavering students less well: group classes differ
only in their proportions of profiles, so a wavering student whose
enrolments happen to be mostly engaged resembles a committed one.

## Uncertainty of the estimates

`parameter_inference()` returns each estimate with its standard error and 95%
Wald interval, from the observed information by default; `vcov_type =
"robust"` gives sandwich standard errors with the students as clusters. The
first ten rows are the profile means.

```{r inference}
inference <- parameter_inference(full)
head(inference, 10)
```

The standard errors of the means are 0.024 to 0.033, and the intervals of the
two profiles are far apart. The last six rows contain the group-level
probabilities.

```{r inference-groups}
tail(inference, 6)
```

The group level is estimated less precisely. The share of mostly disengaged
students is 0.325 (95% interval 0.240 to 0.424); the probability of an
engaged enrolment is 0.164 (0.125 to 0.213) in that class and 0.793 (0.760 to
0.823) in the other.

## Stability across seeds

`sensitivity()` refits the model from several seeds and compares the maxima
and classifications.

```{r sensitivity}
sensitivity(full, seeds = 1:5)
```

All five refits reach the log likelihood of -8313 with identical
classifications (`agreement` of 1).

## Relating the classes to other variables

Entering an external variable in the model can change the classes it is meant to
explain. Three-step methods hold the classes fixed and correct for
classification error (Bolck et al., 2004; Vermunt, 2010). `r3step()`
regresses profile membership on predictors, with the last profile, here the
disengaged one, as reference.

```{r r3step}
r3step(full, data = course_engagement, covariates = "previous_grade")
```

A previous grade one standard deviation higher increases the log odds of an
engaged enrolment by 0.615 (95% interval 0.495 to 0.735), an odds ratio of
about 1.85. `three_step()` compares the mean of a variable across profiles.

```{r three-step}
three_step(full, data = course_engagement, outcome = "previous_grade",
           contrast = "pairs")
```

Previous grades are 0.57 standard deviations lower before disengaged than
before engaged enrolments (95% interval 0.47 to 0.67). Both results are
associations; temporal order alone does not establish an effect of grades on
engagement. One-step alternatives enter predictors in the model
(`profile_covariates` for observations, `group_covariates` for groups);
`fit_staged()` holds the profiles fixed while the group classes are
estimated. The [covariates](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/covariates.html)
and [case study](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/case-engagement-covariates.html)
articles compare these approaches.

## Sampling weights

`weights` names a column of sampling weights, constant within the
independent unit (here `student`). Estimation maximizes a weighted
pseudo-log-likelihood, with weights normalized to sum to the number of
students, and reports Kish's (1965) effective sample size. The example
doubles the weight of the simulated wavering students, as for a design that
sampled them at half the rate, and uses the diagonal structure of the first
model.

```{r weights}
weighted_data <- transform(course_engagement,
                           survey_weight = ifelse(student_type == "wavering", 2, 1))
weighted_fit <- multilpa(weighted_data, vars = vars, id = "student",
                         n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
                         weights = "survey_weight", n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
weighted_fit
```

Weighting changes the prevalence of the classes, not their definition: the
mostly disengaged group class grows from 32.5% to 45.2% of the students and
the engaged profile shrinks from 58.7% to 49.5% of the enrolments, while the
profile means barely change (browsing in the engaged profile 0.525 against
0.540). The effective sample size is 94.5 of 106 students.

For weighted fits, `parameter_inference()` uses sandwich standard errors by
default; `vcov_type = "observed"` is not available, because inverse-information
standard errors do not represent the sampling variance under unequal weights.

```{r weights-inference}
head(parameter_inference(weighted_fit), 4)
```

`weights` is also available in `lta()`, `mixture_regression()` and the other
model families of `multilpa()`. The parametric bootstrap likelihood ratio test
does not accept weighted fits, because its simulations do not reproduce a
sampling design.

## Other options of multilpa()

- **Covariance structures.** `model` takes the fourteen mclust codes (`"EII"`
  to `"VVV"`); `volume`, `shape` and `orientation` set the components
  separately; `local_dependence` frees selected pairs.
- **Missing values.** `missing = "fiml"` uses all observed indicators of
  incomplete rows.
- **Indicator types.** `categorical`, `ordinal` and `count` combine
  categorical, ordinal and count indicators with continuous ones (see the
  [latent class analysis](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/lca.html)
  vignette).
- **Model families.** `family` fits group-class models from raw ratings
  (`"additive"`, `"dispersion"`, `"additive_dispersion"`,
  `"restricted_cross_level"`, `"full_cross_level"`; see the
  [group-class and cross-level](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/additive.html)
  article).
- **Order of observations.** `time` orders each group's observations for the
  sequence tables and `plot_sequences()`; `lta()` models transitions between
  profiles.
- **Centring.** `centering = "person"` subtracts each group's mean, so that
  profiles describe deviations from a group's usual level and group classes
  describe patterns of change; `"grand"` subtracts the sample mean.

## Other tables, plots and functions

The calls below list the other tables, functions and views available for a
fitted model. Each comment states what the call returns.

```{r reference, eval = FALSE}
# Tables: get_results(full, what)
get_results(full, "all")                          # every table, as a named list
get_results(full, "covariances")                  # within-profile residual covariances
get_results(full, "posteriors")                   # one row per observation and profile
get_results(full, "posteriors", format = "wide")  # one row per observation
get_results(full, "group_posteriors")             # one row per group and group class
get_results(full, "classification")               # class sizes and average posteriors
get_results(full, "average_posteriors")           # mean posterior by assigned class
get_results(full, "classification_errors")        # P(assigned class | true class)
get_results(full, "bch_weights")                  # weights for three-step analysis
get_results(full, "residuals")                    # residual correlations within profiles
get_results(full, "information_criteria")         # AIC, BIC and the other criteria
get_results(full, "model")                        # one row describing the fit
get_results(full, "data")                         # the variables used in the fit
as.data.frame(full)                               # the profile table

# Summaries and diagnostics
descriptives(full)                    # indicator summaries with the ICC
descriptives(full, by = "profile")    # the same, by assigned profile
diagnostics(full)                     # every classification diagnostic
report(full)                          # summary, diagnostics and plots together

# Inference and likelihood
parameter_inference(full)             # standard errors and Wald intervals
confint(full)                         # confidence intervals
vcov(full)                            # covariance matrix of the estimates
logLik(full)                          # log likelihood
AIC(full)                             # Akaike information criterion
BIC(full)                             # BIC with the number of groups
nobs(full)                            # number of groups

# Plots: the plot_ functions, each with what = and "all"
plot_views()                                   # every view and what it shows
plot_profiles(full, what = "bars")              # profile means with 95% intervals
plot_profiles(full, what = "heatmap")           # means in standard deviations
plot_profiles(full, what = "all")               # every profile view
plot_diagnostics(full, what = "sizes")          # effective size of each profile
plot_diagnostics(full, what = "entropy")        # per-case classification uncertainty
plot_diagnostics(full, what = "posteriors")     # posterior of each assigned profile
plot_diagnostics(full, what = "avepp")          # average posteriors, assigned by posterior class
plot(full, what = "all")                        # every view this fit supports

# Other functions
sensitivity(full, seeds = 1:10)       # refits under several seeds
```

The [class enumeration](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/enumeration.html)
article covers `enumerate_classes()` and `get_candidate()`; the
[latent transition analysis](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/lta.html)
article covers `lta()`, `get_tna()` and `get_group_tna()`. The evaluation article on the
[package website](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/) covers
`bootstrap_lrt()`, and the covariates article covers `three_step()`,
`r3step()` and `fit_staged()`.

## All tables

`summary()` collects the result tables; `rows` limits the rows printed per
table.

```{r summary}
print(summary(full), rows = 3)
```

## Assumptions

- Profiles have the same means and covariances in every group class.
- Observations are independent given the class of their group, and groups
  are independent. Observations ordered in time, such as a student's course
  sequence, can violate the first condition; `lta()` models the order.
- Under the default diagonal structure, indicators are independent within a
  profile; `covariance_model = "full"`, `model` and `local_dependence` relax
  this, and the `"residuals"` table checks it.
- The numbers of profiles and group classes are chosen from the criteria (see
  the [class enumeration](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/enumeration.html)
  and [model selection](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/model-selection.html)
  articles).

## Reporting

A report of a multilevel LPA states:

- the indicators, their scaling, the grouping variable and the intraclass
  correlations;
- the covariance structure and the evidence for it;
- the candidates compared, the criteria used and the reasons for the chosen
  numbers of profiles and group classes;
- the number of starts, the replication of the best log likelihood and the
  seeds;
- the profile means with standard errors or intervals, the profile
  probabilities of each group class and the class sizes at both levels;
- relative entropy and average posterior probabilities at both levels;
- for external variables, the method (three-step, BCH or one-step) and its
  estimates with intervals.
